question: The proposal on the European Democracy Shield has been portrayed as an ambitious initiative. Unfortunately, there is a major risk that it will extend EU competences into spheres that are traditionally the prerogative of the Member States: elections, civic education, culture and the media.

These areas form part of the democratic identity of each nation and cannot be reshaped using insufficiently-defined EU mechanisms. As it stands, the initiative extends EU competences without giving any clear justification for this and without respecting the principle of subsidiarity.

Romania and the other Member States must remain sole decision-makers when it comes to organising their electoral processes, protecting their information space and maintaining their internal democratic orders. Terms such as ‘disinformation’ or ‘external interference’ are over-vague and may lead to uneven implementation with effects on the press, electoral processes and the quality of public debate.
In these circumstances, it is essential to safeguard national competences to ensure democratic balance. 1.

Does the Commission have a concrete plan for tackling genuine vulnerabilities such as AI-generated false information, cross-border political micro-targeting and the big differences between states in terms of administrative capacities?

Can the Commission guarantee that the Centre for Democratic Resilience does not begin to play a supervisory role over national processes and that its mandate remains strictly limited and clearly defined?
How will the Commission ensure that interventions under the European Democracy Shield do not affect media pluralism?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.2.2026) The European Democracy Shield is designed in full respect of the allocation of competences between the EU and its Member States. It stresses that Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) and disinformation campaigns are often enabled by manipulation techniques, like AI-generated content or AI-driven amplification.

The EU has a strong regulatory framework to address these challenges, including the AI Act1 and the Digital Services Act2. In addition, the Regulation on political advertising3 provides that political advertising must be clearly labelled and include information on who paid for it and whether targeting or ad-delivery techniques have been used.

Building on this framework, the European Democracy Shield sets out further measures, including work with signatories of the Code of Conduct on Disinformation4 to improve the detection and labelling of AI-generated and manipulated content on social media. Furthermore, the Commission announced guidance on the use of AI in electoral processes.

The European Centre for Democratic Resilience will provide a framework for cooperation and coordination among participating Member States and EU institutions and bodies, in full respect of the allocation of competences. Under the European Democracy Shield, support to free and independent media and media pluralism is a priority, building on the EU regulatory and policy framework.

To further support the viability of the media sector, the Commission will assess ways to strengthen the prominence of media services of general interest and modernise advertising rules as part of the evaluation and upcoming review of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive5.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down

harmonised rules on artificial intelligence, OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024. 2 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market for Digital Services, OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, pp. 1–102. 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/900 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 March 2024 on the transparency and targeting of political advertising (OJ L, 2024/900, 20.3.

5 Directive (EU) 2018/1808 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 November 2018 amending Directive 2010/13/EU on the coordination of certain provisions laid down by law, regulation or administrative action in Member States concerning the provision of audiovisual media services (Audiovisual Media Services Directive) in view of changing market realities, OJ L 303, 28.11.2018, pp. 69–92.
